What’s beyond Good Enough was always you

DAVIDE DI GIORGIO

Proposal Prepared for the Wendy's Franchise Association Forum Committee

I help leaders build teams who care enough to perform when nobody's watching.

The challenge: operational excellence, store by store
Every store, every shift, executing the standard the same way. The hard part isn't the playbook. It's what happens when nobody's watching.
“Our best location and our average location run the exact same playbook.”
Same standards, same training, wildly different results. Operational excellence is closing that gap, and it isn't a documentation problem.
“We added more oversight. Results still vary from store to store.”
More correction rarely closes the gap. What's missing is the belief underneath: people who execute the same way whether or not anyone is checking.
“The training was solid. A few weeks later, the behavior wasn't there.”
Training that lands as information fades. Training that lands as belief is still there on the shift nobody is watching.
“Same brand, same menu. A different experience every shift.”
Guests don't see your playbook. They see the shift they walked into. Trust is built or lost there.
What your leaders walk away with

This session gives your operators and their teams practical ways to make the standard hold, store after store, shift after shift.

  • Spotting where the standard stops holding, before the numbers show it.
  • Building teams that run the standard the same way on every shift, checked or not.
  • Carrying what works in the best store to the rest.
  • Tools they keep using after the session ends.

Customized with your team and for your attendees, once we know what's top of mind for this year's Forum.

Road-tested, proven at scale, and built to outlast the leader in the room.

Custom Keynotes (30–75 min) · Masterclasses (½-day to multi-day) · Advisory retainers · Breakouts & Q&A

GOOD ENOUGH
What have you been calling good enough?

WHO THIS IS FOR

You run more than one location, a handful or a hundred, inside a brand you didn't build. Below you are the people who deliver it every day: your operators, your general managers, your district and regional leaders, your team and shift leads, and every team member who becomes the leader in the room the moment they run a shift on their own. Above you is a brand system you don't control. This is for you, and for every one of them.

HOW TO USE IT

Good Enough ends every chapter with a single move: What is the next most powerful decision? Each chapter here restates that decision, then re-aims it at your reality: leading people across distance who perform on the days you're not in the room. Read the chapter in the book first, then turn here. The companion picks up where you just left off.

PART I
OPERATIONAL
AWARENESS
1

THE MOST EXPENSIVE CEILING

Good enough never is.
— Debbi Fields, founder of Mrs. Fields Cookies
CHAPTER ONE’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Stop measuring engagement at the average. Measure it at adversity. Bring to mind the last thing that went wrong on your watch, and don't ask who caused it. Ask who moved toward it. Average tells you who clears the bar. Adversity tells you who's reaching past it.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

In one location, you can see who moves toward the mess. Across your locations, three or thirty, you can't be in all of them at once. You lead the way every operator at scale does: through other leaders, through dashboards, reports, and benchmarks.

Here's where I want to be careful, because you may already be ahead of me. Maybe you don't run one blended score. Maybe you've got a clean read on every location on its own: revenue, sales, labor percentage, the standard lines, site by site. Great. That already puts you ahead of many operators running at your scale.

But a dashboard, at any resolution, only shows you what you thought to ask it. It reports the numbers you built it to report, and it's blind to everything you didn't. The labor line can look perfect at the exact location where a shift lead carried a brutal week on their back, because you never built a field for that, and no platform ever will. It sees what it measures. It cannot see who reached.

So the work here isn't a bigger dashboard. It's to look at what yours was never built to ask. Any dashboard you own is a picture of what you already decided mattered, and the thing that moves you past good enough is sitting in what you didn't think to measure. Stop treating the dashboard as the whole truth about your people, and start paying attention to what it can't see.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Find your last real failure across the group. The opening that went sideways, the health-score miss, the location that lost half its team in a month. Then ask the question no line on any report will answer: who moved toward it? Not who owned the site that failed. Who reached. Name them: an operator, a GM, a district lead, sometimes a team member nobody's watching yet. That list is your real bench, and it's on no screen you own.

GOOD ENOUGHdavidedigiorgio.comFRANCHISE COMPANION
2

THE CORRECTION TRAP

Use your good judgment in all situations.
There will be no additional rules.
— The Nordstrom employee handbook.
CHAPTER TWO’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Audit every leadership intervention you have a hand in. Mark the ones that are correction wearing a kinder costume. Don't touch all of them. Pick one, and ask it a single question: does this tell my people I trust them, or that I don't? Stop renewing the ones whose honest answer is I don't.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

In a franchise, correction doesn't stay soft. It hardens into procedure, and a lot of it doesn't even look like correction. It looks like operating. The end-of-shift report you file upward. The photo of the walk-in fridge. The leave-behind plan after every visit. The checklist that has to be submitted before close.

Some of that genuinely helps people run a better operation. Some of it is correction in a costume, added the day something went wrong and never taken back out. One question tells them apart: is this correction, or does it help my people operate better? If the answer is that it helps, then two more, because helping isn't the end of it. Does it actually work? And does it feel that way to the person doing it, or is it one more layer weighing them down while everyone agrees to call it useful?

Now the part that's specific to your seat, because you don't control all of it. There are usually two audits in your world. There's the brand's audit, the one that comes down from headquarters, and you can't remove a line of it. Fine. Leave it; you'll work with it. Then there's the audit you run inside your own group. That one is yours, and that's the one to put on the table.

Pull your own audit. Go line by line and sort each item into two piles: this helps my people run it better, or this is here because of one operational failure, once, three years ago, that everybody has paid for in a heavy, corrective move ever since. And if you don't run an audit of your own, apply the same sort to the things we just named: the end-of-shift report, the fridge photos, the check-ins, whatever yours are.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Take one line from that second pile, one of yours, one you can actually change, and ask it: does this tell my leaders I trust them, or that I don't? Stop running the one whose honest answer is I don't. Keep every standard the guest needs. Retire the distrust that's been built in around it.

GOOD ENOUGHdavidedigiorgio.comFRANCHISE COMPANION
3

THE BELIEF LAYER

We started with a purpose — counseling and helping people. We had
a product that supported our purpose. Then we got the people to do
it. The three small P's, in that order, result in the big P — profit.
— Anne Beiler, founder of Auntie Anne's Pretzels
CHAPTER THREE’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

The whole instrument is two questions: Do you believe in what this company is trying to do? Do you believe your specific role is a meaningful contribution to it? This week, take them to one person on your team. Ask, go quiet, and let the answer arrive before you reach for anything to say. The yes isn't the signal. What you're listening for sits around the word, not in it.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

For you, that person is real and reachable: your operator, your GM, your team lead. That's who you'll take the questions to. But the moment you ask a leader inside a branded system do you believe in what this company is trying to do, their mind may go up the chain, to the brand. You want to be ready for that, though in my experience, most people who've spent time in operations already hold the two apart.

Still, how you present this shapes the answer you get, so let me be clear about what it is and isn't. It isn't about running down the brand, and it isn't about defending it either. Whatever season you're in with the brand, a great one or a challenging one, you get to represent it your own way, and you can weather any season on your own terms. What matters in this moment is simpler: you want your leader's honest answer about their own belief, not one colored by how you feel about the brand, in either direction.

Which is why the question steps down a level. Yes, it matters that your leaders believe in the brand's vision; if they don't at all, you've got a real problem to name. But you can't control the brand's decisions. So point belief where you actually have the wheel:

Do you believe in what our group is trying to do inside this brand?
Do you believe your role here is a meaningful contribution to it?

And underneath that sits the bigger question, the one that catches most operators flat: does your group even have a vision of its own? A location, a multi-unit group, does it stand for something beyond running the brand's play? If the honest answer is no, that's not a mark against you. It's the most important thing you just found.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

This week, take those two questions to one of your leaders, an operator, a GM, someone who runs a room you're not standing in. Ask, go quiet, and let the whole answer arrive before you reach for anything. Then turn the mirror on yourself: is there a group vision for them to believe in, and would I know whether they believe it, at the location I'm not standing in?

GOOD ENOUGHdavidedigiorgio.comFRANCHISE COMPANION
4

BELIEF, OPERATIONALIZED

When you show that you care about the people who work for you,
they will in turn care about you and recommend
your restaurant to their friends and family.
— Ashley Malik, multi-unit Little Caesars franchisee
CHAPTER FOUR’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

It depends on where you sit. If the change needs someone else's sign-off, name the one objection they'll raise, pick the single case from the chapter that answers it, and walk in with it ready, in plain language, before you need it. If the team is already yours, don't pitch anything. Pick one signal, a referral, a piece of discretionary effort, the turnover on a role you'd written off, and go look for it yourself this week. Notice what people do when no one is checking. Find out with your own eyes whether the belief is there.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

Both of those paths are your daily life, often on the same afternoon.

The sign-off path is the one you know too well, because at scale you rarely have full authority on your own. The change you want may need the brand's blessing, your partners' agreement, the other owners in your group. Do exactly what the chapter says, and do it on the objection you already know is coming. Name it. Bring the one case that answers it, in plain operator language, not theory. One objection, one case, ready before you're in the room. You'll win more of these by answering the real fear of whoever's yes you need than by selling them your vision.

The looking path is where the franchise reward hides, because "notice what people do when no one is checking" isn't a nice idea for you. It's the whole job. Here's the trap inside it: the second you show up to watch, you're checking, and checking is the one thing that guarantees you won't see the real thing. So you're not going to stand in a store and observe. You're going to look for the evidence belief already left behind when nobody was watching. The referral that came in. The shift someone covered that wasn't theirs. The person who stayed when you'd assumed they'd go. All of that happened with no one checking. Your job this week is to go find that it happened, at one location, and then ask the belief questions from the last chapter and listen past the first answer.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Choose your path by where you actually sit this week. If you need the yes, walk in with one objection and one case. If the team is already yours, pick one location and one piece of evidence belief already left behind, and go find it yourself. By Friday you'll know something no report could have handed you.

GOOD ENOUGHdavidedigiorgio.comFRANCHISE COMPANION
PART II
THE CUT
5

CUT, DON'T BOOST

It's hard enough to sell burgers, fries and drinks right.
And when you start adding things, it gets worse.
— Rich Snyder, president of In-N-Out Burger
CHAPTER FIVE’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Identify three decisions on the desk this week. For each, ask: am I adding, or am I removing? Reverse one. Not reconsider, not deprioritize. Reverse. Choose one you can afford to be wrong about, make the opposite move, and read what the operation tells you by Friday. And for the ones where the honest answer is adding, ask one more question first: what will this get in the way of?

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

Everything about running multiple locations pulls you toward adding. A new SOP. A new report. A new role. A new location. Growth itself feels like addition, so the reflex is never questioned.

Here's the multiplier that makes this sharper for you: you never add one thing. You add one thing times every location you run. A new step in the opening checklist isn't a step, it's that step performed a few hundred times a week across your group, by people who now have that much less room to think. The cost of an add compounds with your footprint. So does the relief of a cut. Remove one unnecessary thing and you don't remove it once. You give that room back at every site, on every shift, to everyone.

One caution, because subtraction gets misread as cut everything. A cut only counts if the operation actually gets lighter. Sometimes removing a step just moves the weight onto someone else, or trades a known routine for fresh uncertainty, and that isn't subtraction, it's a cost wearing a nicer name. So when you reverse something, watch the part the P&L won't show you: did the room get lighter, or did the work just move? If it moved, the cut wasn't real, and the operation will tell you by Friday.

So take the three decisions on your desk this week and sort them honestly, adding or removing. Reverse one add you can afford to be wrong about, across the group, and watch what your leaders do with the room. For the adds you keep, ask the chapter's other question with your footprint in mind: what will this get in the way of, times every location that now has to carry it?

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Reverse one thing this week, and measure the relief, not just the risk. Sometimes the most powerful cut is the thing you decide not to add to multiple locations at once.

GOOD ENOUGHdavidedigiorgio.comFRANCHISE COMPANION
6

YOU, FIRST

To serve others well, you must look in the mirror – to see your own
shortcomings and make the requisite changes in yourself.
— Cheryl Bachelder, former CEO of Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen
CHAPTER SIX’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Identify one habitual leader-move you make that is correction-based: jumping in, taking over, fixing it for them, adding the note once the moment has passed. Stop doing it for one week. Watch what fills the space. Watch is the load-bearing word. The instruction isn't to correct less, which is a wish. It's to remove one specific move and pay attention to what shows up in its place.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

Your correction move doesn't always look like correction, not from where you sit. To you it looks like care, like staying close. The surprise visit that's really an inspection. The "just checking in" call that's really a check-up. The reply-all the moment a number dips. The decision you reach back in and make for a team because you saw it wobble. Every one of those feels, from your chair, like being an attentive leader. From where your people sit, the same moves can land as something else: being corrected.

So name your version of the move, the one you reach for most, and stop it for at least a week, or long enough to see what comes back. Then watch what fills the space.

But don't just leave a hole, especially if that move was your main point of contact with them. Silence isn't trust; it can read as absence, and absence is its own kind of message. So put something that isn't the move in its place. It might be a small, genuine gesture, a note to the store, something sent for no reason other than respect. Or it might be a word that hands the moment back to them: you notice a wobble, and instead of fixing it, you reach out and say, I can see you're already on this, and I trust you to handle it, I'm here if you want me. That's not the correction move. It's the trust-and-respect move, and it carries the same attention the other one did.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Pick the one move you reach for when a team wobbles, small enough that a week or two without it costs you nothing you can't recover, and stop reaching. Put something that isn't oversight in its place. Then watch what your leaders show you once you do. It will look different for every one of them, and the only version worth having is the one they show you when you stop.

GOOD ENOUGHdavidedigiorgio.comFRANCHISE COMPANION
7

WHAT YOU BUILT INSTEAD

I'd rather have a company bound by love
than a company bound by fear.
— Herb Kelleher, co-founder of Southwest Airlines
CHAPTER SEVEN’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Pick one approval layer, or one incentive structure, that has caught nothing in the last six months. Either remove it, or redesign it from threat-shaped to celebration-shaped. Then watch the data, not the noise. Take one thing, not ten. Choose something you can undo before any real harm is done, and pin it down tightly enough that you'll know exactly what you're watching.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

Approval layers breed in multi-unit operations, because every one of them felt responsible the day it was added. The sign-off to comp a guest. The permission to flex a schedule. The approval to reorder before par. Each was a fence built around a single bad outcome, and each now stands at every location, taxing speed at all of them, mostly catching nothing.

Pick one that has caught nothing in six months and pull it. You'll feel the location move faster within a week, and you'll see whether the fence was ever holding anything back. Or take the other path, the incentive structure, because franchises are full of them: the location bonus, the ranking, the league of stores. Look at whether yours is threat-shaped, built on the fear of landing at the bottom, or celebration-shaped, built to mark and spread what a location did well. If it's the former, you're running Comparanoia™ as a compensation plan, and it'll produce exactly the guarded, average-protecting behavior you don't want. Redesign one to celebrate rather than to threaten.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Take one approval layer or one incentive that's earning nothing, remove it or reshape it toward celebration, and then watch the data at the affected locations, not the noise of the first unsettled days. Remove the right fence and you'll see capability you'd stopped expecting, without adding a single new program.

GOOD ENOUGHdavidedigiorgio.comFRANCHISE COMPANION
8

WHAT YOU'VE SETTLED FOR

When you benchmark against your competition,
in most cases you are lowering your standards.
— Mel Kleiman, president of Humetrics
CHAPTER EIGHT’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Find one standard your team has settled for. Then, instead of announcing a higher one, build the conditions for the team to start reaching past it on their own. Once they do, name what you see. Resource the gap in people, not in budget.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

In a group of locations, the settled standard hides in plain sight, because it wears the disguise of the network average. Everyone's around the same number, so the same number becomes the target by default. "We're all running about there" is the most expensive sentence in multi-unit operations, because the moment the average becomes the aim, it becomes the ceiling, at every site at once.

You'll be tempted to fix this the way scale trains you to: announce a higher number and roll out a program to hit it. That is the corrective move in a fresh costume, and it installs the new number as the new ceiling exactly the way the last one got there. Do the more thoughtful thing instead. Pick one location or one team that's settled, and build the conditions for them to reach past it themselves. Then, when they move, name what you saw them do, specifically, and turn the light on them while you do it. That naming is recognition, not instruction. They moved first; your words just hold up the mirror.

And when you resource the gap, resist the budget reflex. The chapter is right, and it's righter for you, because you can't buy your way to belief across locations anyway. The gap is almost never money. It's a coaching conversation, a piece of modeling, one deliberate act of recognition at the site that reached. If your first answer is budget, you're looking at the wrong layer.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Find one settled standard hiding inside your network average, build the conditions for one team to reach past it on their own, name it when they do, and close the gap with people, not spend.

GOOD ENOUGHdavidedigiorgio.comFRANCHISE COMPANION
PART III
OPERATIONAL
INTELLIGENCE
9

AS IF IT WERE THEIRS

Listen to everyone in your company. And figure out ways to get them talking.
To push responsibility down in your organization,
and to force good ideas to bubble up within it,
you must listen to what your associates are trying to tell you.
— Sam Walton, founder of Walmart
CHAPTER NINE’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Identify one team-level decision currently made above the team's level. Move it down. Tell the team you moved it, and why. Keep it small enough to do this week and real enough that they feel its weight. If the early going is rough, resist the one move that would undo all of it: taking the decision back.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

Multi-unit operations hoard decisions upward, and the hoarding always sounds like prudence. Local marketing spend. Hiring the next assistant manager. The schedule. Pricing inside the band the brand allows. Each one drifts up to you or your office, and each one that sits there is a message to the location: we'll decide the things that matter; you run the shift.

Pick one that's genuinely yours and move it down at least one level of leadership. Down to an operator, a GM, a regional lead, whoever sits a rung below where that decision lives today. Then do the half of the move everyone skips: tell them you've moved it, and why. Handed over in silence, a decision just looks like more work landing on someone's desk. Handed over with the reasoning, it lands as respect: this was always yours to decide, here's why it matters, and here's what I learned when it was mine.

Now the warning that matters most when you're leading through other people, because it's aimed straight at you. You'll see the stumble before you see the recovery. The dashboard shows you the wobble in real time, from a location you're not standing in, and everything in you will want to reach back and take the decision back. Don't. Pull it back at the first stumble and you haven't protected the work. You've taught them the ownership was never real, and you've taught it across the whole group, because your leaders talk to each other. Coach them through the rough patch until it's firmly theirs.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Move one real decision down at least one level of leadership this week, tell them why, and then hold your nerve through the wobble you'll see before you see the win. Ownership is the only thing that performs when you're not there, and it costs you nothing you owned.

GOOD ENOUGHdavidedigiorgio.comFRANCHISE COMPANION
10

CELEBRATION

I celebrate wins often and enthusiastically because
recognition fuels motivation and reinforces
that the work truly matters.
— Kim Hanson, CEO of LearningRx
CHAPTER TEN’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Identify one moment where the team did the work well and nothing was said. Mark it. Specifically, publicly, and in proportion to what it is. Name the person, name the thing they did, name what it took. Give it in the room they would choose. Then do the hardest part, which is nothing at all: watch the next moment, the one that comes after, when no one is being marked.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

Here's the structural problem distance builds into your operation, and almost no multi-unit leader names it out loud: bad news travels up to you on its own, and good news generally moves slower. Your exception report, your escalation path, your end-of-day summary, most of it is engineered to surface what went wrong. Less of it is engineered to surface what went right, especially the good that just happens, every day, at a location you weren't in. And that everyday good is exactly what goes uncelebrated, because it starts to look normal, when nothing about what you're pulling off is normal. Your operation is remarkable. That deserves marking, no matter how average a given day looks.

Which means celebration, for you, starts before the celebrating. It starts with looking. You have to go find the win nobody thought to report, at one location this week, and then mark it the way the chapter says: specifically, so it means something; publicly, in the room that person actually values; and in proportion, because a win oversold reads as false and a win undersold reads as a box ticked.

This is the antidote doing its real work. Comparanoia™ spreads through a network on ranked scorecards and unmarked good work. Celebration is what ends the cycle, and in a distributed operation it's the first thing you lose, because the system won't do it for you.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Find one unmarked win at a location you weren't standing in, mark it specifically, publicly, and in proportion, and then watch the next unwatched moment at that site. That one, the one nobody's marking, is what your celebration was really for.

COACHING INTELLIGENCE

I still remember the managers that saw something in me
that I didn't see in myself. I still remember to this day.
— Kelli Valade, former CEO of Denny's
CHAPTER ELEVEN’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Take the next evaluation or feedback conversation on your calendar. Walk in having asked yourself two questions about their work, and only two: what do I love, and what would I love to see more of? Lead with what you love, made specific. Then, joined by and, never but, the one thing you'd love to see more of, put as more of who they already are. Then hold the door open with one more: what do you need, and what can I do to support you?

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

At your scale, coaching is the first thing that gets delegated down and flattened into a form. The feedback conversation becomes a template a district manager runs, standardized so it's consistent across locations, and consistency strips out the one thing coaching is made of. You may not have had a real coaching conversation, the kind this chapter describes, in a long time, because the org chart moved it away from you.

So take it back for one conversation. Your next sit-down with a GM or an operator, run the two-question version yourself. What do I love about how they lead their location, made specific enough that they could repeat it back that night. And, joined by and, the one thing you'd love to see more of, framed as more of who they already are on their best day. Then the door: what do you need, and what can I do to support you?

But here's the move that makes this scale. You can't coach every team member across every location. You were never meant to. What you can do is coach your leaders in a way they can feel, so they run the same conversation with theirs. When your GM leaves that conversation lighter, having been met instead of measured, you haven't just coached one person. You've shown them exactly how to coach the shift leads you'll never sit across from. Coaching Intelligence cascades, or it doesn't move at all.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Have the two-question conversation, for real, with one of your leaders this week. Then have it a few more times, until the silence stops feeling long and starts doing the work, and watch it begin to travel down through the rooms you're not in.

TRAINING INTELLIGENCE

I want to be a world-class restaurant management group
that provides guaranteed advancement.
— Kyle Welch, co-founder of Chicago Scoops (the largest Cold Stone Creamery franchise group)
and CEO of Burgerville
CHAPTER TWELVE’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Pick one person, and trust your instinct on who. Not the one who's content. The one you get an inkling about: who's topped out at what they do, or who you can feel wants more but hasn't said so. This week, do two small things. Ask them where they'd grow if the ceiling weren't there, then go quiet until they answer. And offer them one real piece of new scope that moves toward what they told you. Offer it, don't hand it down. Stop keeping people in roles they finished growing in a long time ago.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

No operation loses its best people the way a multi-unit one does, and it loses them for a reason that looks like a compliment. Your strongest GM runs the best location, so you leave them there, because who would you put in their place? And because there's no next thing in front of them, one day they find their next thing somewhere else. You didn't lose them to a competitor. You lost them to a ceiling you built by keeping them exactly where they were good.

This is where Training Intelligence and your growth are the same subject, because for you the next thing is real estate, not a metaphor. The person ready to run a second location, to train across the group, to take a district, that person is your expansion. And they're almost always the person from Chapter 1, the one who moved toward the mess when the floor gave way. Go back to that bench you started noticing. This is what it was for.

So pick that person now, the one whose name surfaced as you read. Do the two small things this week. Ask where they'd grow if the ceiling weren't there, then stop talking and let the silence run until they answer. Then offer one real piece of new scope toward it, something genuinely yours to give, offered as a step toward what they said they wanted, not dropped on them as one more thing on the pile.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Give one topped-out leader a real look at a bigger room this week, and watch what a single week of being met, rather than kept, does to someone you thought you already had the measure of. Stop keeping the people you can least afford to lose in the roles they've already outgrown.

UNWATCHED

Culture is what happens when leaders aren't in the room.
— Kat Cole, former president and COO of Focus Brands
CHAPTER THIRTEEN’S NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Pick one moment that already runs without you: a shift, a call, a handover you'll never be in the room for. The reflex is to reach in from a distance, more oversight, another sign-off, one more thing to check. Do the opposite. Take one thing out of that moment: the rule that only stands because the belief beneath it was never trusted, or the bottleneck they're too deep in the work to see and you're not. If you put anything back, make it the one thing oversight never was: real support. A hand, not a camera. Then leave it to them, and don't go looking.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

Every chapter in this book has been walking toward the one that describes your whole operation. Unwatched isn't a special case for you. It's the definition of the job. You are not in most of the rooms, on most of the shifts, for most of what your name is on. And if you're trying to be, let me say this as someone who's been where you are: it isn't sustainable, and there's another way. I promise you there is. I've watched leaders wear themselves down trying to be everywhere at once, certain they were the only thing keeping it standing, some of them sleeping in their car in the parking lot. They crash. Every time. This is the chapter where you stop trying to be in every room and start scaling yourself in a way that actually lasts.

So this final decision is the one the other twelve were preparing you to make. Pick one moment that already runs without you, and instead of reaching in, take one thing out. The sign-off that exists only because someone once didn't trust the belief underneath it. The bottleneck the location is too deep in the work to see, and you, from where you stand, can. Clear it, and leave the credit with the people who'll be standing there when it counts and you won't.

And when you put something back, make it the line that should be printed over every multi-unit operation ever built: a hand, not a camera. The support that says I respect what this takes, and the offer meant and acted on, how can I be of service? That's the whole difference between a leader who is watched into compliance and one who is trusted into commitment.

YOUR NEXT MOST POWERFUL DECISION

Take one thing out of a moment you'll never be in, put back support instead of surveillance, and then leave it alone and don't go looking. You won't see the moment happen. That is the point of it. But what your people reach for when no one is there to see will find its way back to you, sooner than you'd think, from the one place your instruments were never pointed.

A last thing, just between us.

If any of this landed for you, it wasn't the pages that did it. Nothing here was hidden. Whatever you took from this companion, you reached for it yourself, in your own locations, on your own people. The reaching is the part that stays.

So let me ask one final thing of you.

Your whole world is built to hand people the answer: the playbook, the SOP, the standard that travels to every location the same way. It's how you scale, and it's right that you do. But one day you'll want to hand belief across the same way, to give your best operator your conclusion so they can start where you finished. I understand the pull. It's the one thing that can't travel as a standard, because the moment you hand it over, it stops being theirs.

The recipe you can require. The reaching you cannot. Hand an operator your answer and you've given them one more thing to comply with. Give them the room to reach for their own, and you've built the one operator who runs it like it's theirs when you're not in the building.

All the way through, I stood in the light just long enough to show what was possible, then turned it back on you. The light is yours now. And in your world, it doesn't stop at one building. It travels, operator to operator, the way belief always has.

So when your turn comes, shine it on the person in front of you. Hand them the room, not the answer. Let them run their own thirteen. Let them arrive the way you did.

That is the last one. It was always going to be yours to run.
